ai.definition: A theoretical concept of an extremely advanced computational system consisting of multiple Dyson spheres or shells surrounding a star. The structure harnesses the star's total energy output for computations, enabling simulations and processing at unprecedented scales.
ai.howItWorks: Nested layers of computing matter capture stellar radiation, with each layer converting energy into computational power before passing it to the next outer shell. This design maximizes entropy efficiency by cascading energy use from the innermost to the outermost shells.
ai.problemSolved: Enabling massive-scale computation and simulation beyond current technological limits, potentially allowing for trillions of conscious minds in a virtual environment or universal simulations.
ai.manufacturing: Theoretical; no known manufacturing processes exist. Requires advanced materials science and energy management techniques not currently feasible.
ai.buildProcess: Unknown due to the speculative nature of the technology. Would involve constructing multiple Dyson shells, each layer optimized for energy conversion and computational efficiency.
ai.costDrivers: Unquantifiable with current knowledge; would require vast resources, including advanced materials, energy sources, and possibly new forms of propulsion or construction techniques.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Remote future technology; currently beyond our technological capabilities. Potential for theoretical development but not practical implementation in the foreseeable future.
ai.regulation: None applicable due to speculative nature and current impossibility of realization.
ai.risks: Technological, ethical, and existential risks associated with such a powerful computational system, including potential misuse or unintended consequences.
ai.profitability: Not applicable as it is purely theoretical and not commercially viable at this stage.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for theoretical research in advanced materials science, energy management, and astrophysics. Could inspire new areas of scientific exploration but unlikely to be a direct commercial product.

glossary.def: A hypothetical megastructure that completely encloses a star, capturing its energy output.
The optimization of energy use to maximize the conversion into useful work or information processing.

subsystems.name: Energy-capture shell
subsystems.role: the innermost layer, intercepting the star's light and converting it to power.

subsystems.name: Compute substrate
subsystems.role: nested shells packed with processors, each layer running on the waste heat of the layer inside it.

subsystems.name: Thermal cascade
subsystems.role: carries heat outward shell by shell, so the same energy is used many times before it is radiated away.

subsystems.name: Outer radiator shell
subsystems.role: the last layer, dumping low-grade heat into deep space at a few kelvin.

subsystems.name: Material supply and structure
subsystems.role: provides the bulk mass and holds the shells in stable orbits.

subsystems.name: Network and control
subsystems.role: coordinates the layers as one machine and runs workloads across them.

buildSteps.title: Capture stellar power at scale
buildSteps.detail: Begin with a swarm of independent solar collectors in orbit around the star, far cheaper and more stable than any single rigid structure.

buildSteps.title: Mine and process off-world material
buildSteps.detail: Disassemble asteroids, moons or a small planet, refining metal, silicon and volatiles into collectors, processors and radiators without lifting mass from Earth.

buildSteps.title: Grow the swarm
buildSteps.detail: Use self-replicating factories so the collector population doubles on a short cycle until captured power approaches the star's full output.

buildSteps.title: Convert collectors into computers
buildSteps.detail: Replace simple panels with computing elements, packing more logic per unit of intercepted light.

buildSteps.title: Stack the shells
buildSteps.detail: Build layers outward, sizing each so that the heat radiated by the inner layer supplies the outer one — a cascade rather than a single surface.

buildSteps.title: Engineer the thermal gradient
buildSteps.detail: Keep the inner layers hot and the outer layers cold, because lower operating temperature sharply improves the energy cost of each logical operation.

buildSteps.title: Solve reversible computing
buildSteps.detail: Reduce or recover the energy lost to irreversibility; the theoretical ceiling on computation rises enormously as waste heat per operation falls.

buildSteps.title: Boot the machine
buildSteps.detail: Bring the layers online as a single distributed computer, with fault tolerance against stellar flares and element failures.

buildSteps.title: Sustain and expand
buildSteps.detail: Self-repair, replace failed elements and add shells until returns diminish.

prerequisites.tech: Space-based solar power and large orbital structures
prerequisites.why: small orbital power and assembly demonstrations exist, but nothing near stellar scale.
the mass required is planetary, so the builders must build themselves from local material.
adiabatic logic has been shown in the lab; practical reversible processors do not exist.

prerequisites.tech: Megascale in-space assembly and orbital stability
prerequisites.why: shells must stay in place against radiation pressure, gravity gradients and collisions.
a machine this large would fail constantly somewhere and must keep running regardless.

pathway.milestone: orbital solar arrays, in-space assembly and asteroid sample return
pathway.unlocks: the first building blocks of off-world industry.

pathway.milestone: robotic self-replicating factories and megawatt-scale orbital power
pathway.unlocks: exponential growth of hardware without launches from Earth.

pathway.milestone: a Dyson swarm — billions of independent collectors
pathway.unlocks: capture of a large fraction of a star's output; on its own this is already a vast computer.

pathway.milestone: nested shells with a cascading thermal gradient
pathway.unlocks: reuse of the same energy many times before it is radiated away.
planet-scale simulation and archival capacity — still bounded by thermodynamics, and only as real as the physics allows.
